overview: Both are close biological relationships between two species, but one benefits both partners while the other benefits one at the other's expense.
genZNote: Mutualism: a genuine win-win partnership. Parasitism: one side quietly (or not so quietly) freeloading at the other's cost.

aspects.label: Effect on Both Species
aspects.valueA: Both species benefit from the relationship.
aspects.valueB: One species (the parasite) benefits; the other (the host) is harmed.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Rhizobium bacteria fixing nitrogen for legume roots, receiving nutrients in return.
aspects.valueB: Tapeworm living in a human intestine, absorbing nutrients at the host's expense.

aspects.label: Nature of Dependency
aspects.valueA: Cooperative and often essential for survival of one or both partners.
aspects.valueB: Exploitative — the parasite depends on the host, often to the host's detriment.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Rhizobium in root nodules is a classic NCERT mutualism example, frequently paired with nitrogen fixation questions.
overlay.memoryTrick: Mutualism = mutual win. Parasitism = one-sided cost.
overlay.commonMisconception: Parasitism doesn't always kill the host quickly — many successful parasites evolve to keep the host alive longer, since a dead host often means a dead parasite too.
